title: Replace combinational division with a shared iterative divider
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz, and its 156-cell worst path crosses
forwarding, EX, and the ALU. The ALU currently describes signed and unsigned
quotient and remainder with four combinational / and % expressions. This
deep arithmetic is paid on every clock, including ordinary CoreMark ALU and
address calculations, even when no divide instruction is executing.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz, and its 156-cell worst path crosses

quotient and remainder with four combinational / and % expressions. This

address calculations, even when no divide instruction is executing.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU hardware with one 32-bit iterative unsigned
quotient/remainder datapath and sign normalization at its inputs and outputs.
Start it from the forwarded EX operands, latch the operation and operands,
and hold IF and ID/EX while it runs. Insert EX/MEM bubbles during the wait so
older instructions drain once, then emit exactly one completed DIV/REM result
when the downstream stage can accept it. Keep the existing combinational
RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitutions and let them complete in one cycle. This
should remove the divider from the normal register-to-register critical path;
occasional division latency should cost fewer CoreMark cycles than the Fmax
gain recovers.

Add directed pipeline checks for division after forwarded and loaded operands, division with memory stalls, back-to-back divisions, and exactly one in-order RVFI retirement per operation.

title: Replace combinational division with a shared iterative execute unit
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz. Its 156-cell worst path runs from the
forwarding network through EX/ALU to the data-memory interface. The current
ALU places signed and unsigned division and remainder in the same
combinational result cone as one-cycle address arithmetic, making every
CoreMark cycle pay the divider's timing and area cost even when no divide
instruction executes.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz. Its 156-cell worst path runs from the
forwarding network through EX/ALU to the data-memory interface. The current
ALU places signed and unsigned division and remainder in the same
combinational result cone as one-cycle address arithmetic, making every
CoreMark cycle pay the divider's timing and area cost even when no divide
instruction executes.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU from the one-cycle ALU path into one shared
four-round restoring divider in EX. Each round unrolls eight quotient-bit
steps combinationally and registers the partial quotient and remainder,
breaking the 32-bit divide chain into four shorter timing cones. Launch it
once for each valid divide instruction, hold that instruction and upstream
fetch/decode state while busy, and inject bubbles downstream. When the
result is ready, pass exactly one EX/MEM entry and resume normal execution.
Keep ADD and the load/store address path combinational and independent of
the divider. Complete each divide within the existing formal liveness
window without changing the checks. Handle signed magnitudes, quotient and
remainder sign restoration, division by zero, and INT_MIN / -1 exactly as
RV32M specifies. In RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS builds, use the existing ALU
surrogate results for DIV/REM so the formal specification still matches;
in normal builds, use the iterative result. Retain the existing direct ALU
arithmetic tests and add tests of the actual integrated divider.
Since divides are sparse relative to ordinary CoreMark instructions, the
Fmax gain should outweigh the added divide cycles and reduce LUT use.

title: Tagged branch target buffer for loop and jump prediction
motivation:
The current fetch stage always advances by four bytes. Every taken branch,
JAL, and JALR is corrected in EX, discarding the instruction in decode and
delaying useful fetch. CoreMark repeats short loops and calls across ten
iterations, so the same control-flow PCs recur many times. A small predictor
can remove most of these repeated redirect bubbles while leaving the long
arithmetic path that currently limits Fmax outside the fetch feedback loop.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current fetch stage always advances by four bytes. Every taken branch,
JAL, and JALR is corrected in EX, discarding the instruction in decode and
delaying useful fetch. CoreMark repeats short loops and calls across ten
iterations, so the same control-flow PCs recur many times. A small predictor
can remove most of these repeated redirect bubbles while leaving the long
arithmetic path that currently limits Fmax outside the fetch feedback loop.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 32-entry direct-mapped, PC-tagged branch target buffer in IF. Each
entry holds a target, a valid bit, a two-bit saturating direction counter
for conditional branches, and an unconditional flag for JAL/JALR. A tag
hit predicts the stored target when the counter says taken or the entry is
unconditional; a miss predicts PC+4. Train only when a valid EX instruction
advances, using its resolved target and outcome. Carry the predicted next
PC with the fetched instruction into EX, and redirect only when it differs
from the actual next PC. This comparison must also repair predictions for
illegal, non-control, and misaligned instructions; invalidate stale entries
when a matching PC no longer contains a valid control instruction. Keep the existing
redirect priority over fetch stalls, suppress repeated EX training and
redirects during dmem stalls, and flush younger instructions on a mismatch.
The predictor changes speculative fetch only; retirement and RVFI report
the resolved architectural path.

title: One-hot operand forwarding into EX
motivation:
The iterative divider raised Fmax to 46.079 MHz, but the vendor report
now shows two nearly equal critical paths. Both start at the register-file
BSRAM output and traverse three LUT stages of the EX rs2 forwarding mux.
One path continues through branch redirect and ID control; the other
continues through the multiplier and the data-memory address port.
A change to only one downstream cone would leave the other limiting Fmax.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace each priority-encoded, three-way EX forwarding mux with mutually
exclusive one-hot source enables and a bitwise masked OR of ID/EX,
EX/MEM, and MEM/WB data. Generate the enables directly from register
matches with EX/MEM priority and x0 exclusion. Fold the immediate and
AUIPC source choices into the same one-hot selection for ALU operands,
instead of cascading an additional 32-bit mux after forwarding. Keep
separate post-forward rs1/rs2 values for branches, stores, division
launch, and RVFI. This should reduce the shared data-path depth on both
observed critical paths without changing latency, stall behavior, or
architectural results. Measure the actual Gowin Fmax after implementation.

title: Register instruction fetch to break branch-to-decode feedback
motivation:
The current best core is limited to 46.079 MHz by a 41-cell path that
crosses decode, execute, fetch, hazard control, and the ID/EX register.
IF/ID is presently combinational, so an EX branch decision changes the
instruction and source-register addresses seen by ID in the same cycle.
That long control path is exercised on every clock. The previous structural
divider attempt gained almost no CoreMark cycles and moved the critical
path into arithmetic; the fetch/decode boundary is a better target.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Insert a one-entry registered IF/ID instruction queue between the imem
interface and decode. Capture a fetch only when io_imemReady is high and
the queue is empty or its current entry is consumed in the same cycle;
hold its PC, instruction, and valid bit when decode cannot consume it.
Let an EX redirect take effect only when that EX instruction advances,
then discard the queued wrong-path instruction, set the fetch PC to the
target, and refill the queue from the target after the redirect. Drive
hazard source addresses from the registered queue, gated by its valid
bit, instead of a combinational NOP selected by EX redirect. Keep a
full-rate one-instruction
per cycle path when both buses are ready, and retain the existing EX/MEM
and MEM/WB retirement boundary. This removes the EX-to-IF-to-hazard-to-ID
combinational arc at the cost of one extra taken-branch refill cycle;
a materially shorter clock period should more than repay that cycle cost.

title: Static backward-branch and direct-jump prediction in fetch
motivation:
The iterative-divider champion spends a recovery bubble on every taken branch
and JAL because fetch always selects PC+4 until EX resolves the instruction.
CoreMark has repeated backward loops. The previous tagged target buffer cut
measured cycles by about 6%, but its table and training state cost FPGA
resources. A static prediction can capture the common direct-control-flow
cases with much less hardware on the current fast-divider design.

hypothesis.motivation:
The iterative-divider champion spends a recovery bubble on every taken branch
and JAL because fetch always selects PC+4 until EX resolves the instruction.
CoreMark has repeated backward loops. The previous tagged target buffer cut
measured cycles by about 6%, but its table and training state cost FPGA
resources. A static prediction can capture the common direct-control-flow
cases with much less hardware on the current fast-divider design.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
In IF, inspect the fetched instruction only when imem is ready. Predict the
PC-relative target for every JAL and for conditional branches with a negative
B-type displacement; predict PC+4 for forward branches, JALR, and all other
instructions. Compute the B/J immediates directly from instruction bits and
select either displacement or four as one PC-adder operand, with no BTB, tag
comparison, counter, or table reset. Carry only a predicted-taken bit with
each instruction through ID/EX. EX compares that bit with the resolved
control-flow outcome, after suppressing taken on a misaligned-target trap,
and redirects to its resolved target or PC+4 only on a mismatch. JALR is
predicted sequential and redirects when its valid target is resolved. This
avoids putting a 32-bit predicted-PC comparator on the EX feedback path.
The resolved next PC continues into RVFI. A stalled or invalid fetch
must not advance speculative PC or enter ID/EX. A data-memory stall must hold
prediction metadata and suppress repeated correction; when EX advances, a
correction overrides instruction-memory backpressure and flushes the younger
instruction. This should remove most loop and JAL bubbles while preserving
Fmax better than a stateful target buffer.

title: Isolate memory-port addresses from execute feedback
motivation:
The current champion has two nearly tied vendor timing paths. One runs from
the register-file BSRAM output through the multiplier and general ALU mux to
the data-memory address; the other runs through EX redirect, the flushed
instruction, and back to the register-file read address. Neither memory
port needs these dependencies: loads and stores need only rs1 plus their
immediate, and a flushed instruction's source-register reads have no
architectural effect. A local trial of both changes raised placement-option
0 Fmax from 50.41 to 54.961 MHz with only 15 extra LUTs and 32 extra FFs.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current champion has two nearly tied vendor timing paths. One runs from
the register-file BSRAM output through the multiplier and general ALU mux to
the data-memory address; the other runs through EX redirect, the flushed
instruction, and back to the register-file read address. Neither memory
port needs these dependencies: loads and stores need only rs1 plus their

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Remove unnecessary EX-dependent logic from both memory address ports.
Give EX/MEM a dedicated effective-address field, computed from forwarded
rs1 plus the decoded immediate independently of the general ALU result.
Use that field in MEM for the data-memory address, byte offset, alignment,
and RVFI memory address; keep alu_result for arithmetic writeback. Feed the
register-file read ports directly from raw fetched rs1/rs2 bit positions,
while continuing to decode and latch the flushed NOP for invalid or
redirected fetches. Wrong-path register reads are harmless because the
ID/EX valid and control state still comes from the existing flushed
instruction. This removes the multiplier-to-data-memory path and
redirect-to-register-file path together, without changing pipeline cycles,
bus handshakes, register contents, or RVFI retirement. A local implementation
passed all five cocotb suites, both cosim programs, and 53 single-retire
formal checks. Full FPGA evaluation measured 54.575 MHz median and 128.12
fitness versus 49.551 MHz and 116.33 for the champion, with identical
4,259,618 CoreMark cycles.

title: Separate data-memory address generation from the general ALU
motivation:
The champion's worst timed path starts at the register file, crosses EX and
the general ALU, and ends at the FPGA data memory. The ALU result selection
shares that path with shifts and M-extension arithmetic even though every
load and store needs only base-plus-offset. A prior registered fetch stage
shortened another path but added enough refill cycles to lose fitness.

title: Hashed bimodal direction predictor for conditional branches
motivation:
Static backward-taken prediction is the current winner, but a CoreMark
retirement trace shows 111,175 incorrectly predicted conditional branches
across 529,588 branches. Returns account for only 13,735 instructions, so
a return-address stack has much less upside. A 64-entry, two-bit direction
table indexed by a simple XOR of PC bit groups reduced trace-replayed
direction misses to about 41,500. It needs no target or tag storage, unlike
the earlier BTB whose large circuit sharply reduced Fmax.

hypothesis.motivation:
Static backward-taken prediction is the current winner, but a CoreMark
retirement trace shows 111,175 incorrectly predicted conditional branches
across 529,588 branches. Returns account for only 13,735 instructions, so
a return-address stack has much less upside. A 64-entry, two-bit direction
table indexed by a simple XOR of PC bit groups reduced trace-replayed

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the present instruction-bit target calculation for JAL and branches.
For conditional branches only, use a 64-entry table of two-bit saturating
direction counters, indexed by PC[7:2] XOR PC[13:8]. A reset-cleared valid
bit per entry selects the current backward-taken rule on the first use of
an index; a valid entry predicts taken when its counter's high bit is set.
Train the indexed counter from a valid branch only when EX advances, using
the architecturally redirectable outcome after target-misalignment handling.
Initialize an untrained entry to strongly taken or strongly not taken from
that first outcome. Preserve the carried predicted-taken bit, the current
one-bit outcome mismatch check, and the resolved RVFI next PC. The table
stores no targets, so a mistaken direction still recovers through the
existing redirect, including during instruction stalls. This should
remove most direction misses while keeping the EX comparison and fetch
target adder unchanged; the small table limits area and timing exposure.

title: Use explicit flip-flop banks for the integer register file
motivation:
The current worst path begins at a register-file BSRAM output, traverses
execute forwarding and the ALU, and ends at the EX/MEM result register.
The 32-word register file is small enough to use local flip-flops within
the FPGA area budget. A local trial with explicit per-register write
enables reached 60.444 MHz median Gowin Fmax and 141.9 fitness, versus
54.575 MHz and 128.12 for the champion, with identical CoreMark cycles.
All five cocotb suites and 53 single-retire formal checks passed.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Implement x1 through x31 as separate 32-bit flip-flop banks with explicit
address-equality write enables, while keeping x0 constant and preserving
the two asynchronous read ports and same-cycle write bypass. This prevents
BSRAM inference for the register file and lets Gowin place read sources

title: Partition execute with a registered multiplier and valid-only squash
motivation:
The champion has two nearly tied critical path families at 23.49 ns:
forwarding through a DSP multiplier into EX/MEM, and register-file data
through branch resolution into the wide ID/EX flush. Shortening only one
leaves the other at roughly the same Fmax. A reference run of the exact
2K -O3 CoreMark binary counted 93,960 multiplies in 2.92 million timed
retirements, so adding one cycle per multiply costs about 2.2% of the
current 4.26 million timed cycles. The prior registered fetch queue cost
considerably more cycles because it added a redirect refill bubble.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Partition the EX boundary into an ordinary one-cycle datapath, a
registered-operand multiply path, and a one-bit wrong-path squash token.
Capture post-forward operands for MUL, MULH, MULHU, and MULHSU and place
exactly one completed product into EX/MEM on the next edge. Hold younger
instructions and bubble EX/MEM while the product is pending, giving a
blocked data-memory operation priority. Remove hardware products from
the core's ordinary ALU selector. In parallel, stop using EX redirect to
clear the entire ID/EX payload or mux a NOP into the fetched instruction:
capture the instruction fields normally and clear only its valid bit on
redirect, fetch stall, or load-use bubble. Qualify all EX side effects,
branch decisions, memory requests, divider/multiplier launches, and
load-use detection by that valid bit. A mispredicted branch still creates
the same one EX bubble and sets fetch PC to its target on the same edge.
This cuts both measured path families without changing the common-case
pipeline depth or branch recovery latency. Preserve ALTOPS substitutions,
RV32M signed high-product semantics, ordered RVFI retirement, and bus
backpressure behavior.

title: Operand-aware conditional branch prediction in fetch
motivation:
The current static backward-taken rule mispredicts about 111,175 of
529,588 conditional branches in a measured CoreMark trace. A 64-entry
bimodal table reduced misses but added enough FPGA logic to lower Fmax,
and its 1.6% cycle gain did not beat the champion. Many branches can
instead use their already available register values to predict the
exact outcome without a learned table or target storage.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current static backward-taken rule mispredicts about 111,175 of
529,588 conditional branches in a measured CoreMark trace. A 64-entry
bimodal table reduced misses but added enough FPGA logic to lower Fmax,
and its 1.6% cycle gain did not beat the champion. Many branches can
instead use their already available register values to predict the
exact outcome without a learned table or target storage.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the existing PC-relative target calculation and static rule as a
fallback. For a valid conditional branch at the fetch address, compare
its source operands using the existing register-file read ports and
registered EX/MEM or MEM/WB forwarding where appropriate. Use that
exact condition as the prediction only when neither source depends on
an unresolved ID/EX writer, an EX/MEM load, or a stalled operation;
otherwise use backward-taken. Decode only legal branch funct3 values.
Carry the selected predicted-taken bit into EX as today, where the
existing resolved-outcome mismatch redirects and preserves RVFI PCs.
Compute the branch target and PC+4 in parallel with the operand check,
placing only a final direction mux on the fetch PC path. This should
remove recurring forward-taken and backward-not-taken recovery cycles
without the state, update network, or target mux of a BTB. A redirect
must retain priority over all fetch stalls, and no prediction may
retire or modify architectural state.
